newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tensions high after reported Russian-Chechen clash.
newsitem.headline: Tensions high after reported Russian-Chechen clash.

text.p: Tensions between Moscow and Chechnya rose on Tuesday after a bomb killed two people at a southern Russian railway station and a skirmish was reported between Russian police and Chechen fighters.

Partagen Andriyevsky, commander of Russian forces in the north Caucasus, told Interfax news agency that police had fought a gun battle for more than an hour with 20 fighters who crossed from separatist Chechnya into the southern region of Dagestan.
He said there were deaths in the night-time clash near the Dagestan settlement of Andi. Two Russian policemen were injured.
A later Interfax report said the Chechens suffered unspecified "losses" before retreating into Chechnya.
Andriyevsky said all checkpoints on the administrative border between Dagestan and Chechnya were being closed from 0200 GMT on Tuesday.
The clash appeared to be one of the worst since a ceasefire between Russian and Chechen forces was signed last August.

A Reuters cameraman who visited the Gerzel crossing point, about 50 km (31 miles) east of the Chechen capital Grozny, said the border was still open at 0400 GMT and that border troops knew nothing of the reported clash.
Cars were moving freely across the border.

But relations between Moscow and Chechnya were clearly strained after Russia blamed Chechen separatists for Monday's bomb blast at the railway station in the Russian spa town of Pyatigorsk, about 130 km (80 miles) northwest of Chechnya.

A spokesman for the Federal Security Service (FSB) in Moscow said a man died instantly when the bomb exploded near the ticket office in the first-floor waiting room. A teenage girl died of her wounds during the night, he added.
The spokesman said 19 other people were injured, six seriously. The blast wrecked the station roof, blew out all the windows and caused major damage inside the building.

Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said he suspected a "Chechen link" and the FSB spokesman said two women had been detained as suspects. He said both were from the Caucasus region and NTV television said they were Chechens.
Security measures were stepped up in Russia's southern areas.
Chechen leaders denied any involvement in Monday's blast or in a bomb explosion at Armavir railway station in southern Russia last Wednesday which also killed two people.

The separatist leaders, who fought a nearly 21-month conflict with Russian troops that killed tens of thousands before last August's ceasefire, said Russian security forces were to blame. This implied some Russian forces wanted to stir tensions.
"I categorically declare that the Chechen side did not take part in the terrorist acts on Russian territory," Chechen Vice President Vakha Arsanov told Ekho Moskvy radio station.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Monday he was deeply concerned and made clear relations with Chechnya would deteriorate sharply if a Chechen link was confirmed and the separatist leaders did not crack down in their region.

"The Interior Ministry and Federal Security Service leadership have enough forces and resources to take uncompromising actions and initiatives to stop terrorist acts," presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Interfax.
Chechen leaders still want full independence for their mainly Moslem region, which remains awash with weapons. Moscow has ruled out independence for Chechnya.
Radical guerrilla commander Salman Raduyev has vowed to attack Russia's rail network and other targets to press the campaign for independence.
Itar-Tass news agency said Raduyev had claimed responsibility for last week's explosion at Armavir, but more moderate Chechen leaders doubted he was behind the blast.
